title: IGNITE AI Quick Log FAB: Scan, Describe, Voice, Activity, Weight
description: IGNITE AI Quick Log FAB explained—Scan/Snap Track, Describe, Voice, Activity, and Weight—and when to use each capture path so logging never dies in a “where do I tap?” friction loop.

body: The center Quick Log FAB is the product’s nervous system. It is where capture begins: camera modes for meals and labels, describe and voice-style inputs when photos are the wrong tool, activity for training, and weight for scale check-ins. Learning it once removes half of “where do I tap?” friction forever.

People who only ever use one path burn out when that path fails—dark restaurants, known leftovers, or a gym session that is not food. The FAB is designed as a switchboard, not a single button with a single religion.
This guide maps each FAB destination, when to choose it, and how it feeds Home rings and Progress without turning every entry into a project.

sections.heading: Scan / Snap Track: camera-first capture
body: Choose Scan when the object is in front of you and vision or packaging helps: meal photos, nutrition labels, barcodes, and drinks. It is the mixed-plate and grocery lane.
Always plan an edit glance before confirm. The FAB gets you into capture; your review makes the diary true—especially on oils and servings.

sections.heading: Describe: when you already know the meal
body: Describe shines for repeats, leftovers, and simple plates you can name in a sentence. It is often faster than photographing a known bowl under bad lighting.
Be specific: quantities, cooking fat, brand names if relevant. Vague describe inputs create vague macros. Saved meals can still be faster when the text would be identical daily.

sections.heading: Voice-style input: hands-busy moments
body: Voice helps when your hands are messy or you are walking out of a restaurant. Speak the meal like you would text a coach: foods, amounts, extras.
Verify the transcript before confirm. Voice errors on numbers—“fifty” versus “fifteen”—are expensive. The FAB path is speed with a mandatory sanity check.

sections.heading: Activity: training belongs in the same app
body: Log workouts from the FAB so food and training share one timeline. That pairing matters for recovery conversations and for avoiding double-counting burned calories in careless ways.
Enter sessions the same day. Retrospective workout fiction helps nobody, especially if Friends auto-share training.

sections.heading: Weight: scale and progress context
body: Use Weight entry for consistent check-ins—same time of day when possible. Pair with Progress trends rather than reacting to one noisy morning after salty food or alcohol.
If you take progress photos as part of your routine where the product supports them, keep them private and consistent in lighting. They are optional context, not daily punishment.

sections.heading: Choosing a path in under five seconds
body: Package in hand → barcode/label via Scan. Messy plate → meal photo via Scan. Known leftover → Describe or saved meal. Gym done → Activity. Morning scale → Weight. That decision tree should become reflex.
If you hesitate longer than the meal is interesting, you will skip logging. Speed of path choice is part of adherence.

sections.heading: FAB hygiene on busy weeks
body: Keep reminders pointing at the FAB moment, not at abstract motivation. The ping should mean “open Quick Log now.”
When one mode breaks—camera issues, OCR fail—rotate to Describe immediately. The FAB’s power is redundancy.

sections.heading: Where Premium meets the FAB
body: Core AI capture inside Snap Track is Premium by design. The FAB still orients you; Premium unlocks the heavy vision and related AI tools that make Scan powerful on mixed meals.
That honesty matters in guides like this: the switchboard is for everyone to learn, and the AI lanes are a paid compute stack—not a hidden forever-free infinite scanner fantasy.

sections.heading: Bottom line
body: Master the Quick Log FAB as a switchboard: Scan for camera modes, Describe/Voice for known or hands-busy meals, Activity for training, Weight for check-ins.
Open IGNITE AI’s FAB with a clear lane each time—and let rings fill from confirmed reality instead of from navigation confusion.

title: Smart Pantry in IGNITE AI: Cook From What You Already Own
description: What Smart Pantry does in IGNITE AI—keep ingredient context close to Snap Cook and meal logging so dinners match the fridge you own, not a fantasy shopping list you will never actually buy.

body: Meal plans fail when they assume a supermarket you did not visit. You cannot cook seared salmon and six fresh herbs if the fridge holds eggs, rice, and a tired bag of spinach. Smart Pantry exists to keep “what I own” in the same universe as cooking ideas and logging—so suggestions and decisions respect inventory reality.

A pantry feature is not a magic chef. It is context. When ingredient awareness sits beside Snap Cook and your diary, you waste less food, skip fewer planned dinners, and stop logging imaginary recipes you never made.
This guide explains how to think about Smart Pantry, how to keep it updated without bureaucracy, and how it pairs with IGNITE AI cooking and logging tools for ordinary weeks.

sections.heading: Why inventory context beats fantasy plans
body: Diet planners that ignore the fridge create aspirational menus and empty diaries. When dinner collapses into delivery, the plan was theater. Pantry-aware flow starts from constraints: protein on hand, carbs on hand, sauces on hand.
Constraints sound limiting; they are liberating on Tuesday night. Fewer options, faster cooking, higher chance you will log what you actually ate.

sections.heading: What to keep in a living pantry list
body: Track staples that change decisions: proteins, grains, wraps, key sauces, oils, and produce that expires soon. You do not need to catalog every spice jar unless that helps you personally.
Update when you shop and when you finish items. A stale pantry list is how the feature becomes ignored chrome.

sections.heading: Shopping trips as pantry resets
body: After grocery runs, add new staples and remove what you stopped buying. Barcode and label scans during unpacking can feed both the diary and your sense of what entered the house.
Avoid logging the entire haul as eaten food. Purchasing is not consuming. Pantry is inventory; Snap Track meals are intake.

sections.heading: Snap Cook with what you own
body: When cooking ideas respect pantry context, you are more likely to prepare a meal you can photograph and log accurately. The loop is: see ingredients → cook → Snap Track the plate → save if it will repeat.
If Cook suggests something missing a critical item, treat that as a signal to update pantry or to shop with intent—not to force a recipe that guarantees takeout later.

sections.heading: Waste less, log more
body: Expiring produce should drive near-term meals. Logging those meals closes the loop between waste reduction and macro honesty. Throwing away food you “planned” helps neither budget nor Progress.
Batch-cook pantry proteins into containers you can save as weekly staples. Pantry plus meal prep is a force multiplier.

sections.heading: Keep pantry maintenance light
body: Five minutes after shopping beats a monthly archaeology project. If maintenance feels heavy, shrink what you track to the decision-critical items only.
Shared households should agree who updates inventory. Conflicting pantry fiction—“we have chicken” when you do not—creates false Cook confidence.

sections.heading: Pantry versus food log boundaries
body: Do not blur eating with owning. Oil in the pantry is not oil on tonight’s rings until you pour it. The diary remains sacred for intake; pantry remains sacred for possibility.
When you cook, the oil leaves pantry context and enters the meal log via your edit. That handoff is the whole point.

sections.heading: Where IGNITE AI Smart Pantry fits
body: Use Smart Pantry to keep ingredient context close to Snap Cook and the logging tools you already trust—Snap Track for the finished plate, saved meals for repeats. Premium AI cooking and capture tools do more good when they are aiming at food you can actually make.
The product honesty carries over: AI features are not an excuse for fantasy grocery lists. Pantry grounds them in your kitchen.

sections.heading: Bottom line
body: Smart Pantry aligns cooking and logging with the fridge you have. Keep it lightly updated, cook from constraints, and log the plate that resulted.
In IGNITE AI, let pantry context feed Snap Cook—and let Snap Track record reality—so plans stop assuming a supermarket that never happened.

title: How to Scan Nutrition Labels with IGNITE AI Snap Track
description: How to scan nutrition labels with IGNITE AI Snap Track—when label photos beat barcodes, how to avoid per-100g traps, and how quick edits keep packaged macros honest before you confirm.

body: Barcodes are fast until they are wrong, missing, or tied to a reformulated recipe. Nutrition label scanning exists for the moments when the panel on the package is the source of truth—imports, store brands, damaged UPCs, or multipacks that confuse scanners.

Label mode is still a draft. Glare, wrinkled film, and tiny fonts create misreads. Your job is to photograph clearly, check serving math, and edit before confirm so the diary does not inherit a per-100g disaster as a “serving.”
This walkthrough covers framing, serving traps, when to prefer barcode versus label, and how IGNITE AI Snap Track fits a grocery-plus-pantry workflow.

sections.heading: When label mode beats barcode
body: Use label photos when the scan misses, returns the wrong flavor, or shows macros that disagree with the printed panel. Also use it for products without a usable code—farmer’s market jars, some international snacks, bakery nutrition stickers.
Prefer barcode when the match is clean and you already trust the entry. Label mode is the recovery tool and the truth check, not a slower default for every yogurt cup.

sections.heading: Framing the panel
body: Fill the frame with the nutrition facts, avoid glare, and keep text sharp. Flatten curved bottles as much as practical. If the label wraps, take a second shot of the serving size line.
Confirm language and units. Mixing mL and grams, or misreading “per 100g” as “per serving,” is how macros explode or collapse.

sections.heading: Serving size traps
body: Always map the label serving to what you will eat. A bag that lists 2.5 servings is not “one scan = one snack” unless you truly eat one serving. Multipacks hide this constantly.
Powders, oils, and concentrates are frequent offenders. Log the scoop or tablespoon you used, not the whole container the OCR noticed.

sections.heading: Per 100g versus per serving
body: Many international labels emphasize per 100g. If the app interprets that block as your meal, you may log a fraction or a multiple of reality. Check which column became the diary entry before you save.
When ambiguous, weigh the portion once and apply the per-100g math deliberately. One careful correction teaches a staple forever.

sections.heading: Edit checklist after OCR
body: Verify product identity, calories, protein, carbs, fat, and serving count. Fix brand name if you care about re-findability. Then save the corrected item as a staple if you buy it weekly.
If sugar alcohols or fiber affect how you personally count net carbs, apply your own rule consistently after the raw label is captured. Consistency beats ideology wars inside one diary.

sections.heading: Store aisle workflow
body: Scan barcode first for speed. If anything looks off against the package in your hand, switch to label mode immediately—before you leave the aisle and lose the evidence.
For meal-prep cartons you assemble at home, label the components you buy; photograph the finished container later as a meal. Do not ask one label to represent a mixed bowl.

sections.heading: Failure modes and fallbacks
body: If OCR fails, type key macros from the panel or use describe mode with the numbers in front of you. A manual two-field fix is better than abandoning the entry.
Report persistent misreads with product details via in-app bug flows when appropriate. Field labels teach the system more than silent rage.

sections.heading: Where IGNITE AI Snap Track label mode fits
body: In IGNITE AI, Snap Track keeps label capture beside barcode and meal photo so you can change weapons without changing apps. Confirm only after serving math looks human.
Premium unlocks that AI capture stack—an honest gate for compute-heavy reading. Use it when packaging is the truth; switch to photo when the meal leaves the package and hits a plate.

sections.heading: Bottom line
body: Label scanning is how you win when barcodes lie or vanish—provided you frame clearly and police serving size. Per-100g confusion is the silent assassin.
Use IGNITE AI Snap Track label mode as the packaged-food recovery path, edit once, save staples, and keep the aisle from becoming a guessing game.

title: Track Drink Calories in IGNITE AI (Lattes, Smoothies, Alcohol)
description: Why drink calories wreck “clean” food days—and how IGNITE AI Snap Track drink logging captures lattes, smoothies, and alcohol so beverages hit the same daily rings as lunch and dinner.

body: Solid-food diaries with invisible drinks are fan fiction. A “clean” chicken-and-rice day plus two large lattes, a smoothie, and evening wine can erase the deficit while the meal log still looks disciplined. Liquid energy is easy to forget because it does not feel like chewing a meal.

IGNITE AI Snap Track includes drink logging so beverages compete for the same daily budget as food. That is not pedantry; it is how weekly averages stay connected to reality when café culture and social drinks are normal.
This guide covers coffee drinks, smoothies, sodas, and alcohol—how to capture them quickly, what to edit, and how to stop beverages from silently owning your Progress chart.

sections.heading: Which drinks deserve priority
body: Anything with milk, sugar, syrup, juice, cream, protein powder, or alcohol belongs in the diary. Black coffee and plain sparkling water are usually rounding errors; flavored “just coffee” often is not.
Smoothies and meal-replacement shakes are meals in a cup. Log them with the seriousness of lunch, including add-ins like peanut butter and full-fat yogurt.

sections.heading: Café lattes and “healthy” menus
body: Milk type, size, and syrup pumps dominate the total. A large oat-milk mocha is not the same object as a small Americano. If the café publishes nutrition, use it; otherwise estimate high on syrup and milk.
Protein coffees still need logging. Extra protein is useful; extra sugar and milk fat still count. Drink mode plus edits beats guessing “about 100.”

sections.heading: Smoothies and blender calories
body: Homemade smoothies should be logged from ingredients when you can—fruit, milk, powders, nut butters. Photo of a finished cup helps as a reminder but ingredients tell the truth.
Shop smoothies vary wildly. Prefer label or published nutrition when available; otherwise bias upward and save a corrected custom drink for the place you revisit.

sections.heading: Alcohol as a liquid line item
body: Log beer, wine, and cocktails in drink flows as you go. Mixers matter. A spirits drink is not automatically low-calorie once juice and soda enter.
Pair alcohol logging with the night-out food protocol: late plates still need photos. Drinks alone rarely explain the whole weekend average.

sections.heading: Timing: log when the cup arrives
body: Enter the drink when you order or when it hits the table. End-of-day reconstruction forgets the mid-afternoon refill. Notifications can help if café runs are your blind spot.
If you share a pitcher or bottomless brunch drinks, log your portion deliberately. “We shared” without a fraction is how deficits vanish.

sections.heading: Editing without fake precision
body: You do not need laboratory certainty. You need directional honesty that keeps weekly averages useful. When unsure between two sizes, pick the larger once and learn your café defaults.
Save frequent orders as repeats. The second time should take seconds. Friction is what makes people “forget” the latte.

sections.heading: How drinks interact with rings and rollover
body: Drink entries should move calorie and carb rings like food. If they do not appear to, check that you confirmed the entry. Rollover plans that ignore liquid spend will feel mysteriously tight on Mondays.
On flexible days, decide whether the bank funds dinner, drinks, or both. Funding both without weekday undershoots is just a surplus.

sections.heading: Where IGNITE AI drink logging fits
body: Open Snap Track drink mode for lattes, smoothies, and alcohol so beverages land on the same Home rings as meals. Use label mode when a bottle has a panel; use photo for elaborate café creations when it helps you remember to edit syrups.

Premium unlocks the AI capture stack that makes these modes practical at speed. The product stance is deliberate: liquid calories are first-class diary citizens, not an afterthought toggle buried in settings.

sections.heading: Bottom line
body: If it pours and it has calories, it belongs in the log the same day. Café drinks and alcohol are common silent deficit killers.
Track them in IGNITE AI drink logging beside your meals—so Progress reflects the week you actually drank, not the week your solid food pretended you lived.

title: Auto-Share Meals and Workouts to IGNITE AI Friend Groups
description: How IGNITE AI auto-share pushes meals and workouts into Friend group feeds—what to share, what to keep private, and how to build accountability without posting manually after every log.

body: Accountability rarely fails because people lack motivation slogans. It fails because sharing takes too many taps after a meal you already struggled to log. Auto-share exists for that exact friction: when a meal or workout is confirmed, it can land in your Friend group feed without a second posting ritual.

IGNITE AI Friends are private circles built around real diaries—plates, sessions, and reactions—not empty chat rooms. Auto-share preferences sit on top of that: you choose whether meals, workouts, or both flow into the groups you trust. The point is social pressure on autopilot, not a public performance for strangers.

This guide walks through when auto-share helps, when it becomes noise, how to set boundaries, and how to pair it with Share Cards for Stories. None of this replaces coaching judgment; it is a workflow for people who already know that being seen mid-week keeps logs honest.

sections.heading: Why manual sharing dies by Wednesday
body: After dinner you are tired, the log is done, and “post to the group” feels optional. Skip it three nights and the feed goes quiet; quiet feeds stop reminding anyone. Manual sharing rewards the most energetic members and abandons the people who need accountability most.
Auto-share flips the default. Logging becomes the share. Your circle sees consistency without you remembering a social chore on top of nutrition tracking.

sections.heading: What auto-share should include (and exclude)
body: Many people share workouts freely and keep snacks quieter—or reverse that if training feels personal and meals are the accountability lever. Preferences exist so you are not forced into all-or-nothing broadcasting. Start narrow: one group, one content type, one week.

Exclude anything you would not want misread out of context: medical notes, extreme restriction language, or client data if you coach. Friend groups are private, not encrypted therapy rooms. Share the proof that helps the circle, not every micro-detail of your day.

sections.heading: Setting expectations with your circle
body: Tell the group what auto-share means: “You will see my dinners and lifts unless I pause it.” Without that, people may assume every post is a request for critique. Agree on reaction norms—encouragement first, advice only when asked.
If someone joins who is not ready for food feeds, create a second quieter group or keep them on workout-only sharing. Privacy design is social design, not only a toggle.

sections.heading: Meals: share the log, not the lecture
body: A shared meal works best as a simple artifact: what you ate, roughly how it fit the day, maybe one honest note. Long moral essays about “being good” train the group to perform. Short, boring consistency trains the group to keep logging.

When a night is messy, still share if that is the rule. Unlogged chaos is what kills weekly averages; visible imperfect dinners are data your friends can relate to without turning the feed into a shame contest.

sections.heading: Workouts: proof of training rhythm
body: Auto-sharing Exercise logs shows frequency and effort without requiring a separate fitness social app. Pair food and training in the same circle so recovery conversations stay grounded—high training weeks need honest intake, not silent deficits.
If you train with partners, shared sessions become gentle attendance pressure. Missed days are visible; so are comebacks. That visibility is the product, not a leaderboard trophy.

sections.heading: Pause, mute, and damage control
body: Travel, illness, or a stressful week may call for a temporary pause. Pausing is healthier than flooding the feed with junk entries or disappearing entirely. Come back with a normal log rather than a dramatic apology post.
If you shared something you regret, remove or clarify quickly and reset preferences. Auto-share should feel like a seatbelt, not a trap. Control stays with you in preferences—use it.

sections.heading: Share Cards versus auto-share
body: Auto-share is for private Friend feeds. Share Cards are for outward Stories and posts when you want a polished snapshot. Use both without confusing them: Cards market or inspire; auto-share keeps your inner circle honest.
Creators especially should keep Friends private and Creator Groups separate. Dumping every private meal into an audience feed is a privacy mistake dressed as engagement.

sections.heading: Where IGNITE AI fits the accountability job
body: In IGNITE AI, enable auto-share from Friends preferences so confirmed meals and workouts can flow into the groups you choose. Combine that with ordinary logging—Snap Track for plates, Exercise for sessions—so the feed is fed by real diary work, not staged content.
Premium still gates the heavy AI capture tools; social sharing does not replace honest logs. The win is fewer abandoned days because someone will see the gap—and you will too.

sections.heading: Bottom line
body: Auto-share turns finished logs into Friend-group proof without a second posting shift. Choose what leaves your device, set group norms, and pause when life needs quiet.
If willpower alone keeps failing mid-week, turn on IGNITE AI auto-share for the circle that already cares—and let consistency become the default post.

title: Creator Groups vs Private Groups in IGNITE AI: Which Should You Use?
description: Creator Groups versus private Friend groups in IGNITE AI—who can create what, how feeds differ, Creator Program requirements, and which room fits accountability versus audience community.

body: IGNITE AI has two social shapes that look similar in a feed and behave very differently in real life. Private Friend groups are for people you know: small accountability, shared meals, shared workouts, mutual trust. Creator Groups are audience rooms led by approved creators, centered on the creator’s logging rhythm and community standards.

Choosing wrong creates awkward privacy leaks or empty “communities” that nobody posts in. Choosing right keeps Friends intimate and puts scale where it belongs—behind Creator Program approval, not a casual tap.

This comparison is practical: setup, who can create, how joining works, content norms, and when to run both without mixing mental models. It is product guidance, not legal advice on influencer contracts.

sections.heading: Private groups: the inner circle
body: Private groups exist for friends, training partners, couples, or a tiny challenge squad. Everyone is roughly a peer. The feed should feel safe enough to show a chaotic takeout night without performing for an audience.

Create these when accountability is the job. Keep membership invite-based and small enough that silence is noticeable. Auto-share preferences shine here because the audience already has context on your goals.

sections.heading: Creator Groups: audience-scale rooms
body: Creator Groups are built for approved creators whose followers want an in-app place to see meals, workouts, and community posts tied to real product use. The gravitational center is the creator’s cadence, not a random chat of strangers without a host.
Creating a Creator Group requires Creator Program approval. Joining as audience typically uses search or invite codes. That gate exists so “creator community” is not a free-for-all spam surface.

sections.heading: Feed purpose and content standards
body: In private groups, norms can be informal: react, cheer, ask questions. In Creator Groups, publish clear rules early—what belongs, what gets removed, how critique works. Audience rooms collapse without moderation basics.
Lead with logs and training proof, not endless text threads. The product advantage is nutrition and workout context sitting beside conversation, not replacing a generic social network.

sections.heading: Privacy boundaries you should not blur
body: Never treat a Creator Group like a private diary. Assume audience members can screenshot. Keep client check-ins, medical details, and unpaid personal drama out of creator feeds.
Likewise, do not drag audience members into your private Friend group without consent. Mixing those rooms is how trust breaks—even if the UI makes resharing feel easy.

sections.heading: Which should you use this month?
body: Use private groups if your only goal is sticking with two to eight people. Use a Creator Group if you already educate publicly and want a durable in-app home for superfans who actually log.
Many creators run both: Friends for real life, Creator Group for audience. The mistake is using one room for both jobs and then wondering why either feels wrong.

sections.heading: Joining, invites, and first-week setup
body: For private groups, invite people who already agreed to be seen. Pin a one-line purpose. For Creator Groups, seed early posts so the first scroll is not empty—meals, workouts, and a pinned rules card beat a barren launch announcement.
Mention the Group on social only after it looks alive. Empty rooms convert curiosity into bounce; living rooms convert lurkers into loggers.

sections.heading: How Creator Program ties in
body: Creator Groups sit inside the Creator Program stack: approval, personalized codes, audience annual Premium pricing where offered, and often complimentary Premium so you can demo Snap Track honestly on camera.
The Group does not replace your code. It complements it—community retention beside acquisition. Keep Refer a Friend and Creator Program stories distinct when you explain benefits publicly.

sections.heading: Where IGNITE AI fits either path
body: Both room types attach to real IGNITE AI logs and optional Share Cards. Private groups pair well with auto-share. Creator Groups pair well with educational posting and polished Cards for external platforms.
Premium still matters for AI capture quality in either room: communities built on vague estimates feel weak. Log well, then socialize the proof.

sections.heading: Bottom line
body: Friends groups are for your circle; Creator Groups are for approved creators building audience community inside IGNITE AI. Different trust models, different content rules, different creation gates.
Pick the room that matches the job—or run both deliberately—and keep private proof out of public feeds so accountability and audience growth do not cancel each other.

sections.heading: Metrics and goals without false precision
body: Enter weight, height, and goals as honestly as you can. The model is a starting estimate, not a lab metabolic test. You will refine with Progress averages over weeks.
Pick a fat-loss pace you can live with beside your real schedule. Heroic deficits look brave on day one and cruel on day twelve.

sections.heading: Diet focus and training context

If you are injured or inconsistent, say so through activity choices. Onboarding that assumes five gym days when you manage two creates rings you will resent.

sections.heading: AI plan generation as a first draft
body: When onboarding generates a plan, treat it as a structured starting point. Diet planner swaps exist for a reason — grocery reality always wins eventually.
